items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845) would be approximately 25 in 1870 — his first appearance as an adult. He may still be living in Thomas Flynn's household or may have formed his own. FamilySearch collection 1438024 (United States Census, 1870; 38.5M indexed persons) is free and fully indexed: search Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — his last known location — first, broadening to all of Pennsylvania if no match. If Thomas Flynn appears in the same household, this is adult co-residence evidence corroborating the inferred parent-child relationship established in 1850 and 1860. Search variant spellings Flinn and Flin.

Thomas Flynn (I2) has no sources attached — he is known only from inferred co-residence in the 1850 and 1860 censuses and a secondary mention on Patrick's death certificate. If Patrick has formed his own household by 1870 and Thomas is not found there (pli_006), search for Thomas Flynn independently in collection 1438024 in Schuylkill County. Expected age approximately 50–65. Finding Thomas establishes his age, birthplace, and remaining household composition; any other children still present bear directly on q_001. Search variant spellings Flinn and Flin.

The 1880 U.S. census (collection 1417683; 50.2M indexed persons) is the first federal census to record each person's explicit relationship to the head of household. If Thomas Flynn is living with Patrick by 1880, the relationship column will distinguish 'father' from lodger or neighbor — making this the highest-value census year for q_001. Patrick (~35) would likely be head of his own household. Search Schuylkill County first; broaden to Pennsylvania if needed. Variant spellings: Flinn, Flin.

If Thomas Flynn is not found in Patrick's 1880 household (pli_008), search for Thomas independently in collection 1417683. Thomas would be approximately 60–70. An 1880 enumeration with explicit relationship labels would show who Thomas is living with and in what capacity, either corroborating or complicating the parent-child relationship inferred from 1850 and 1860. This is the only record type in this plan where the relationship column directly labels kin ties, so both the Patrick-led and Thomas-led search are worth executing.

Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, d. 1908) would be approximately 55 in 1900 and almost certainly still living. The 1900 census (collection 1325221; 76.2M indexed persons) records birth month and year and — crucially — each person's father's and mother's birthplaces, which bear directly on q_001. Note: the 1890 census was almost entirely destroyed in a fire and is not searchable. Thomas, if born ~1810–1820, would be approximately 80–90 in 1900 and may or may not appear in Patrick's household; even if absent, Patrick's parents' birthplaces as he reported them provide independent evidence. Search Schuylkill County; broaden to Pennsylvania if needed. Variant spellings: Flinn, Flin.

If FamilySearch returns no result for Patrick Flynn in 1870 — due to transcription errors on the Flynn/Flinn surname — search Ancestry's 1870 census as a cross-check before concluding the year was a nil result.

A missed 1880 record would leave the question of whether Thomas Flynn is labeled as Patrick's father unresolved.

Fallback for pli_010. Ancestry holds an independent index of the 1900 U.S. census, which also records parents' birthplaces. If FamilySearch (pli_010) does not return Patrick Flynn in 1900, search Ancestry before treating the year as a nil. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.
